newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.S. poll on Croatian leader raises questions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. poll on Croatian leader raises questions.

text.p: A U.S.-sponsored poll showing Croatian President Franjo Tudjman with 81 percent approval inexplicably contrasts with popular discontent at his authoritarian rule, analysts said on Friday
The survey was carried out by the U.S. Information Agency (USIA), a branch of the State Department, and released to Croatia's state-run media on Wednesday.

"USIA polls have proven rather accurate in the past so we have no reason to question the results," said a U.S. diplomat, after sceptical questions were asked about USIA methods. The polling procedure has not been made public.
Analysts were amazed the president should rate so high when private polls show his nationalist government has sunk to its lowest esteem since Tudjman led Croatia to independence in 1991.

The USIA poll was conducted last month at an atypical moment in Croatian public life. Tudjman, 74, was in a U.S. hospital for reported cancer treatment while Zagreb was rocked by mass demonstrations against the government.

Protesters were upset at state attempts to shut down an independent radio station, declining living standards, and corruption that has allowed a politically connected elite to grow rich from fraudulent privatisation.
Fifty-three percent of 987 Croat adults in the USIA's face-to-face poll said they had a "very favourable" and 28 percent a "somewhat favourable" opinion of Tudjman.

"Tudjman has always been more popular than his party as he is regarded here as the larger-than-life Father of the Nation. The poll confirmed that. Sympathy for a seriously ill president probably boosted him in the poll too," a Western diplomat said.

"But Tudjman's high rating was still surprising -- and contradictory when set against the unpopularity of government media. How can you be so sceptical about government media and at the same time stoutly support the president?"

Some asked why a U.S. agency released a poll buoying Tudjman just days after he denounced "foreign influences" for supposedly trying to topple him, including the U.S.-based Soros Foundation whose local chief was held by police for questioning on Friday.

"The timing is weird. What is the USIA doing? You had Tudjman criticising every kind of foreign influence and then the biggest one, the Americans, put out a poll supporting him," said one veteran diplomat.

"Whoever was responsible for this, the poll has clearly been used by the government to help itself at a time when it is in big trouble," he said, referring to the state media's triumphant flaunting of the poll findings.

In contrast to the support for Tudjman, the poll reported three-quarters of its respondents said there was bias in state television and radio, which is run by the ruling HDZ party and treats Tudjman with fawning deference.
The poll said 88 percent backed the development of an independent media. Tudjman, an ex-communist general, has hounded Croatia's liberal free press for years.
"Disenchantment with various policies associated with Tudjman's tenure is evident to everyone in Croatia," said Chris Cviic, a Croatian scholar based in London.

"That applies to the deteriorating economic situation, the amount of corruption in public life and Croatia's low image abroad -- which has bothered Croats quite a bit -- resulting from various repressive policies under Tudjman."
